title: The Meter Reader #1: The Reading
author: Wren Aldous & Piotr Sable
blurb: A municipal utility inspector walks up a stairwell to take a reading and finds that the building has opinions about being measured. Forty pages, stapled, printed on whatever the Ironside press had that month. The one everybody has heard of and nobody has actually read, largely because the film came later and was worse.
source: Scanned from the Mint Condition reading copy, Ironside Street, Coldwater. In-universe fiction.

chapters.title: Page One — The Ground Floor
chapters.text:
PANEL ONE. A door. Grey, institutional, half a number missing from it, the ghost of the missing digit still legible in cleaner paint. Nothing else in the panel. It takes up a third of the page and it is doing nothing, and that is the point: the artist wanted you to stand in front of it for a second before anybody arrives.

CAPTION: Tuesday. The building had been quiet for eleven days, which the district office recorded as "no fault reported."

PANEL TWO. A man from behind. Municipal tabard, reflective strip across the shoulders gone chalky. A clipboard held down at his side the way a man holds a thing he has carried for twenty years. We do not see his face. We will not see his face for six pages, and when we finally do it will be an anticlimax, and the artist knew that too.

METER READER: Utilities.

PANEL THREE. Same door. Still shut.

METER READER: Utilities. It's the reading.

PANEL FOUR. A hand comes into the panel from off-page and rests flat on the door. Not knocking. Just resting.

CAPTION: You do not have to let a meter reader in. You have never had to let a meter reader in. There is no law that says so and there never was. What there is instead is a form, and the form has a box on it, and the box says ACCESS REFUSED, and the box has consequences that nobody has ever written down anywhere you could read them.

PAGE TWO.

PANEL ONE. The door is open. We did not see it open. This is the first of the book's three cuts and it is the one people argue about — whether he was let in, or whether the artist simply declined to draw the part where a door stops being a door.

INTERIOR: a hallway. Wallpaper in a pattern that was chosen by somebody who is dead. A pram folded against the wall. A bicycle with no chain. The kind of hall that is all objects belonging to people who are elsewhere.

PANEL TWO. A woman in the kitchen doorway, arms folded. She is drawn with more line-weight than anything else on the page. In a book this cheaply printed that is the only way to say IMPORTANT, and it is used exactly four times in forty pages.

WOMAN: You're not the usual one.

METER READER: No.

WOMAN: Where's the usual one.

PANEL THREE. He looks at the clipboard. He does not look at her.

METER READER: I've got the reading.

PANEL FOUR. Wide. The kitchen. A pot on the stove with nothing under it. A calendar with the days crossed off in a hand that got worse and then stopped. On the far wall, low, half-hidden behind a chest freezer that has been pushed in front of it: the meter cabinet, painted over four times, its little glass window wiped clean in a perfect circle by somebody's thumb.

CAPTION: Every flat in Coldwater has one. It is the only object in your home that the city considers to be its own, sitting inside the only place the city agrees is yours.

PAGE THREE.

PANEL ONE. Close on the meter face. Six digits on white drums. The last one is caught between numbers, half of a 4 and half of a 5, which is a thing real meters do and which almost no artist bothers to draw.

PANEL TWO. His hand with a pencil, writing the figure on the form. The pencil is blunt. There is a groove worn into his finger.

WOMAN (off-panel): That's not right.

PANEL THREE. He keeps writing.

METER READER: It's what it says.

WOMAN (off-panel): Nobody's been using anything. There's nobody here to use anything.

PANEL FOUR. He looks up. Still from behind, still no face — but the tilt of the head has changed, and the artist has moved his shoulder down by about four millimetres, and it reads, on cheap paper, at arm's length, as a man deciding whether to say the next thing.

METER READER: I know.

PANEL FIVE. Black panel. One line of white text, small, centred, with a lot of space around it.

CAPTION: The number had gone up every week for eleven weeks, in a flat where the calendar stopped, and it was his job to write it down, and he had written it down, and he had gone home, and he had come back, and it had gone up again.

chapters.title: Pages Four to Twelve — The Rising Figure
chapters.text:
PANEL ONE. The stairwell. Vertical panel, the full height of the page, drawn looking up: eleven flights of switchback rail receding into a skylight that is not there any more, just the frame and the sky. He is a small figure at the bottom. This is the image everyone reproduces, and it is on the cover of every reprint, and the artist reportedly hated it and considered it the laziest page in the book.

CAPTION: Flat 2. Flat 6. Flat 9. Flat 14.

PANEL TWO. A door. Grey. Half a number.

METER READER: Utilities.

PANEL THREE. A different door. Also grey. A different missing digit.

METER READER: Utilities.

PANEL FOUR. A third door, and now the artist has stopped drawing the walls around them, so the doors float on white, and the sequence has become a rhythm rather than a place.

METER READER: It's the reading.

PAGE FIVE — SIX. A double-page spread of meter faces. Thirty-one of them, in a grid, each one drawn with its own dirt and its own crack and its own painted-over cabinet. Under each, in the same blunt pencil hand, the figure. The figures go up. They go up in every flat. They go up in the two flats that are boarded from the outside.

CAPTION: The district office ran a check on the substation and found it sound. The district office ran a check on the trunk main and found it sound. The district office wrote to the building and the letters came back marked NO SUCH RESIDENT, thirty-one times, which the district office recorded as "no fault reported."

PAGE SEVEN.

PANEL ONE. Night. He is at a kitchen table in his own flat, which is drawn exactly like the first flat, down to the wallpaper. This is the second cut, and it is the one that is actually good: nothing in the art tells you it is his flat and not hers. You work it out three panels later and you go back.

PANEL TWO. The forms spread out. His hands flat on either side of them.

PANEL THREE. Close on one form. The pencil figure. Beside it, in ink, in a different hand, in the margin where nobody is supposed to write: a second figure. Larger.

PANEL FOUR. His hands have not moved.

CAPTION: He had not written that.

PAGE EIGHT.

PANEL ONE. The meter cabinet in his own kitchen. Painted over four times. A perfect circle wiped clean in the little glass window.

PANEL TWO. Closer.

PANEL THREE. Closer. The drums. Six digits. The last one caught between numbers.

PANEL FOUR. Closer still, and now we are inside the glass, and the drums are the whole panel, and the artist has done something with the halftone screen that makes them look wet.

PANEL FIVE. Full page, no border. The number.

It is a very large number. It is printed in a typeface that appears nowhere else in the book. Readers have counted the digits and there are nineteen of them, and there is no unit given, and the enduring argument about this book is whether the missing unit is the joke or the horror.

PAGE NINE.

PANEL ONE. He is writing it down.

PANEL TWO. He is still writing it down.

PANEL THREE. He is still writing it down. The pencil is shorter.

CAPTION: It is not the reader's job to be alarmed. It is the reader's job to read.

PAGE TEN — TWELVE. The stairwell again, the same vertical panel, the same rail, the same absent skylight — except that now the figure at the bottom is going up, and on each page he is one flight higher and one size smaller, and on the last of the three pages he is not in the panel at all, and the number of flights has not changed.

chapters.title: Pages Thirteen to Forty — The Face
chapters.text:
PANEL ONE. The top landing. A door that is not grey. It is the only warm colour in the book after page three, and the printing on the original run was badly registered so the colour sits about two millimetres to the left of the door, which every reprint has faithfully reproduced because collectors would riot otherwise.

PANEL TWO. There is no number on it and no space where a number was.

METER READER: Utilities.

PANEL THREE. Nothing.

METER READER: It's the reading.

PANEL FOUR. Nothing.

PANEL FIVE. He puts his hand flat on the door and rests it there.

PAGE FOURTEEN.

The whole page is the inside of the top flat and it is the reason people who have read this book will not shut up about it to people who have not.

It is a room with thirty-one meter cabinets on the walls. Every one of them painted over four times. Every one with a perfect circle wiped clean. Every one running. In the middle of the room there is a kitchen table with forms spread out on it and a blunt pencil laid across them, squared to the edge. There is one chair. There is nobody in it.

The art here abandons the cheap open linework of the rest of the book entirely and goes to a dense crosshatch, thousands of strokes, and on the original press it clogged, and the top third of the page on most surviving copies is a solid grey-black smear. The publisher never fixed it. There is a strong argument, which the artist made loudly for the rest of her life, that it should never be fixed.

PAGE FIFTEEN.

PANEL ONE. He sits down.

PANEL TWO. He picks up the pencil.

PANEL THREE. He begins to write.

PAGE SIXTEEN through PAGE THIRTY-NINE.

Twenty-four pages of forms.

No figures, no dialogue, no captions, no panel borders. Each page is a facsimile of a municipal utility form, filled out in blunt pencil, one flat per line, thirty-one lines a page. The addresses are real Coldwater addresses. The dates run backwards. On page twenty-two, on line nine, the handwriting changes for a single entry and then changes back, and nobody has ever satisfactorily explained what that entry says.

People skip these pages. People have always skipped these pages. The book is designed to be skipped here — the thickness of the skipped part is doing the work, in the hand, physically, and that is a thing a comic can do and almost nothing else can.

PAGE FORTY.

PANEL ONE. Small, top left, alone on an otherwise empty page.

His face.

It is an ordinary face. Fifty-something, tired, shaved yesterday. It is not frightened and it is not haunted and there is nothing behind the eyes that shouldn't be. It is the face of a man at work.

CAPTION: They send someone every week. They have always sent someone every week. Nothing is wrong with the building.

PANEL TWO. The door. Grey. Half a number missing, the ghost of the missing digit still legible in cleaner paint.

METER READER (off-panel): Utilities.

THE END

—

[Inside back cover, all editions:] LETTERS. Write to us. We read everything and we answer what we can. We are told the second issue will be along when it is along.

There was no second issue.
